content_voiceover: This slide organizes hemoglobinopathies by their functional mechanism, a favorite board framework. High-oxygen-affinity hemoglobins shift the dissociation curve left, so they hold onto oxygen too tightly and deliver less to tissues. That drops the P50, triggers a compensatory rise in EPO, and produces an autosomal dominant erythrocytosis, but importantly with a normal PaO2 and no splenomegaly, which is the clue that separates it from other causes of polycythemia. Low-oxygen-affinity hemoglobins do the opposite, shifting the curve right with an elevated P50 and 2,3-DPG, producing anemia, cyanosis, and a low pulse ox saturation. Unstable hemoglobins are structurally altered so the heme-globin interaction breaks down, forming Heinz bodies and hemichromes that drive chronic hemolysis, classically presenting with dark urine or pigmenturia. Finally, M hemoglobins, either acquired or hereditary cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency, oxidize heme iron from ferrous to ferric, causing methemoglobinemia. The board pearl here is the pseudocyanosis pattern: brownish or slate-colored skin without true dyspnea or clubbing, a low pulse oximetry reading, but a paradoxically normal or high PaO2 on blood gas, because the oximeter is being fooled while the dissolved oxygen is fine.
keypoints: High O2-affinity Hb: ↓P50, left shift, AD erythrocytosis, normal PaO2
Low O2-affinity Hb: ↑P50/2,3-DPG, right shift, anemia + cyanosis
Unstable Hb: Heinz bodies/hemichromes → hemolysis, dark urine
M(met)Hb: cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency → Fe3+ heme
Classic clue: ↓SaO2 by pulse ox but normal/high PaO2 on ABG
keypoint_voiceover: Remember the four mechanisms: high-affinity hemoglobin shifts the curve left causing erythrocytosis with a normal PaO2; low-affinity hemoglobin shifts right causing anemia and cyanosis; unstable hemoglobins form Heinz bodies leading to chronic hemolysis with dark urine; and M hemoglobins from cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency oxidize iron to the ferric state. The classic board clue for methemoglobinemia is a low pulse oximeter reading paired with a normal or high PaO2 on arterial blood gas.
